'''Simon Conway Morris''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (born 6 November 1951) is an English [[palaeontologist]], [[evolutionary biologist]], and [[astrobiologist]] known for his study of the [[fossils of the Burgess Shale]] and the [[Cambrian explosion]]. The results of these discoveries were celebrated in [[Stephen Jay Gould]]'s 1989 book ''[[Wonderful Life (book)|Wonderful Life]]''. Conway Morris's own book on the subject, ''[[The Crucible of Creation]]'' (1998), however, is critical of Gould's presentation and interpretation.

Conway Morris held the Chair of Evolutionary Palaeobiology in the [[Department of Earth Sciences, University of Cambridge]] between 1995 and 2019 and is now Emeritus Professor.<ref>2025, December 01). ==Biography==

===Early years===
Conway Morris was born on 6 November 1951 in [[Carshalton]], Surrey. He was brought up in London, England,<ref>{{cite web | title=The Nature of Nature | url=http://www.designinference.com/documents/2000.04.nature_of_nature.htm | publisher=Conference on the Role of Naturalism in Science | date=12 April 2000 | access-date=20 February 2010}}</ref> and went on to study geology at [[Bristol University]], achieving a First Class Honours degree. He then moved to [[Cambridge University]] and completed a PhD at [[St John's College, Cambridge|St John's College]] under [[Harry Blackmore Whittington]]. He is professor of evolutionary palaeobiology in [[University of Cambridge Department of Earth Sciences|the Department of Earth Sciences]] at Cambridge. He is renowned for his insights into early [[evolution]] and his studies of [[paleobiology]]. He gave the [[Royal Institution Christmas Lectures|Royal Institution Christmas Lecture]] in 1996 on the subject of ''The History in our Bones''. He was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] at age 39, and was awarded the [[Charles Doolittle Walcott Medal|Walcott Medal]] of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1987<ref name=Walcott>{{cite web|title=Charles Doolittle Walcott Medal |url=http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_walcott |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=14 February 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513235831/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_walcott |archive-date=13 May 2011 }}</ref> and the [[Lyell Medal]] of the [[Geological Society of London]] in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lyell Medal |url=https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/About/Awards-Grants-and-Bursaries/Society-Awards/Lyell-Medal |access-date=2022-05-16 |website=The Geological Society of London}}</ref>

===Work===
Conway Morris is based in the Department of Earth Sciences at the [[University of Cambridge]] and is best known for his work on the Cambrian explosion, the Burgess Shale fossil fauna and similar deposits in China and Greenland. In addition to working in these countries he has undertaken research in Australia, Canada, Mongolia and the United States. His studies on the Burgess Shale-type faunas, as well as the early evolution of skeletons, has encompassed a wide variety of groups, ranging from [[Ctenophora|ctenophores]] to the earliest [[vertebrates]]. His thinking on the significance of the Burgess Shale has evolved and his current interest in [[Convergent evolution|evolutionary convergence]] and its wider significance&nbsp;– the topic of his 2007 [[Gifford Lectures]]&nbsp;– was in part spurred by [[Stephen Jay Gould]]'s arguments for the importance of contingency in the history of life.

In January 2017, his team announced the discovery of ''[[Saccorhytus]]'' and initially described it as an early member of the [[deuterostome]]s which contain a diverse group of animals including vertebrates,<ref>{{cite web | title=Bag-like sea creature was humans' oldest known ancestor | url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/bag-like-sea-creature-was-humans-oldest-known-ancestor | access-date=31 January 2017| date=30 January 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Han|first1=Jian|last2=Conway Morris|first2=Simon|last3=Ou|first3=Qiang|last4=Shu|first4=Degan|last5=Huang|first5=Hai|title=Meiofaunal deuterostomes from the basal Cambrian of Shaanxi (China)|journal=Nature|volume=542|issue=7640|pages=228–231|year=2017|issn=0028-0836|doi=10.1038/nature21072|pmid=28135722|bibcode=2017Natur.542..228H|s2cid=353780}}</ref> but subsequent analysis reclassified this taxon as a member of the [[protostome]]s, probably within the [[ecdysozoa]]ns.<ref>{{cite journal |journal=Nature |title=Saccorhytus is an early ecdysozoan and not the earliest deuterostome |author=Yunhuan Liu |author2=Emily Carlisle |author3=Huaqiao Zhang |author4=Ben Yang |author5=Michael Steiner |author6=Tiequan Shao |author7=Baichuan Duan |author8=Federica Marone |author9=Shuhai Xiao |author10=Philip C. J. Donoghue |date=2022 |volume=609 |issue=7927 |pages=541–546 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-05107-z |pmid=35978194 |bibcode=2022Natur.609..541L |s2cid=251646316 |url=https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/454e7bec-4cd4-4121-933e-abeab69e96c1 |hdl=1983/454e7bec-4cd4-4121-933e-abeab69e96c1 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

====Burgess Shale====
Conway Morris' views on the [[Burgess Shale]] are reported in numerous technical papers and more generally in ''[[The Crucible of Creation]]'' (Oxford University Press, 1998). In recent years he has been investigating the phenomenon of evolutionary convergence, the main thesis of which is put forward in ''Life's Solution: Inevitable Humans in a Lonely Universe'' (Cambridge University Press, 2003). He is now involved on a major project to investigate both the scientific ramifications of convergence and also to establish a website ([https://mol.org// www.mol.org/]) that aims to provide an easily accessible introduction to the thousands of known examples of convergence. This work is funded by the [[John Templeton Foundation]].

====Evolution, science and religion====
Conway Morris is active in the public understanding of science and has broadcast extensively on radio and television. The latter includes the [[Royal Institution]] Christmas Lectures delivered in 1996. A Christian, he believes in [[theistic evolution]] and opposes [[intelligent design]] but believes in an [[God|intelligent designer]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kenigsberg |first=Amos |date=2005 |title=Evolving Truth |url=https://www.bu.edu/sjmag/scimag2005/features/evolution.htm |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=Triplepoint |publisher=[[Boston University]]}}</ref> He has participated in science and religion debates, including arguments against intelligent design on the one hand and [[materialism]] on the other. In 2005 he gave the second Boyle Lecture.<ref name=boylelecture>{{cite web | title=Boyle Lecture 2005: Darwin's Compass | publisher=St Mary-le-Bow | url=http://www.stmarylebow.co.uk/?download=boylelecture05.pdf#/boyle-lecture-2005/4535725162 | year=2005 | access-date=20 February 2010}}</ref> He has lectured at the [[Faraday Institute for Science and Religion]] on "Evolution and fine-tuning in Biology".<ref>{{cite web | title=Summer Course No. 1 – Unit 1: The Big Questions in Science and Religion – St Edmund's College, Cambridge: July 16–22, 2006 | url=http://www.st-edmunds.cam.ac.uk/faraday/Short_course.php?Course_selection=2&Mode=Old | publisher=The Faraday Institute for Science and Religion | year=2006 | access-date=20 February 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607195531/http://www.st-edmunds.cam.ac.uk/faraday/Short_course.php?Course_selection=2&Mode=Old | archive-date=7 June 2011 | df=dmy-all }}</ref> He gave the [[University of Edinburgh]] Gifford Lectures for 2007 in a series titled "Darwin's Compass: How Evolution Discovers the Song of Creation".<ref>{{cite web | title=News & Events | url=http://www.ed.ac.uk/news/070206gifford.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080409234638/http://www.ed.ac.uk/news/070206gifford.html | publisher=The University of Edinburgh | archive-date=9 April 2008 | access-date=20 February 2010}}</ref> In these lectures Conway Morris explained why evolution is compatible with belief in the existence of a God.<ref>The points cited are taken from the official abstracts of the {{cite web | title=Gifford Lectures 2006 – | url=http://www.hss.ed.ac.uk/Admin/Gifford/documents/SimonConwayMorristitleandabstracts3.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070320010203/http://www.hss.ed.ac.uk/Admin/Gifford/documents/SimonConwayMorristitleandabstracts3.pdf | publisher=University of Edinburgh | archive-date=20 March 2007| access-date=20 February 2010}}</ref>

He is a critic of [[materialism]] and of [[reductionism]]:

<blockquote>That satisfactory definitions of life elude us may be one hint that when materialists step forward and declare with a brisk slap of the hands that this is ''it'', we should be deeply skeptical. Whether the "it" be that of [[Richard Dawkins]]' reductionist gene-centred worldpicture, the "universal acid" of [[Daniel Dennett]]'s meaningless [[Darwinism]], or [[David Sloan Wilson]]'s faith in group selection (not least to explain the role of human religions), we certainly need to acknowledge each provides insights but as total explanations of what we see around us they are, to put it politely, somewhat incomplete.<ref name=boylelecture/></blockquote>

and of scientists who are militantly [[Antireligion|against religion]]:

<blockquote>the scientist who boomingly – and they always boom – declares that those who believe in the Deity are unavoidably crazy, "cracked" as my dear father would have said, although I should add that I have every reason to believe he was – and now hope is – on the side of the angels.<ref name=boylelecture/></blockquote>

In March 2009 he was the opening speaker at the [[Biological Evolution: Facts and Theories]] conference held at the [[Pontifical Gregorian University]] in Rome, as well as chairing one of the sessions. The conference was sponsored by the Catholic Church.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.catholicnews.com/data/stories/cns/0900998.htm|archive-url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20090310223435/http://www.catholicnews.com/data/stories/cns/0900998.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=10 March 2009|access-date=6 July 2011|title=CNS Story: Organisms' common ancestry aids medical research, says biologist}}</ref> Conway Morris has contributed articles on evolution and Christian belief to several collections, including ''The Cambridge Companion to Science and Religion ''(2010) and ''[[The Blackwell Companion to Science and Christianity]] ''(2012).
